title: Build a Body Plan
principle: Building a body is done by local rules, and part of it is taking things away.

t: You have all four pieces now. Lay out an animal — and then find out where it goes wrong.
One cell, position from gradients, identity from Hox genes, and difference from selective reading. Assemble a body plan, then watch it get stress-tested.
sub: Every missing piece breaks it in its own particular way.
Each omission produces a different and diagnosable failure, which is what makes this a test.

t: Put each part in the job it does. Any part fits any slot, so it is on you.
Assign each mechanism to its role. Placement is unconstrained — only the assignment is graded.

label: Makes enough cells to work with
Tells each cell where it is
Says what kind of thing to build there
Makes cells actually different from each other

name: Have something to build with
Proliferation
pass: Enough cells to make an animal out of.
fail: One cell is not a body plan.
Without proliferation there is no field of cells for any pattern to be imposed on.

name: Know which end is which
Axis
pass: There is a front and a back.
A polarity axis is established and readable.
fail: A featureless ball of cells. Nothing has a position.
No gradient, no coordinate. Every cell is in the same situation as every other, so nothing can differ systematically.

name: Build the right thing in each place
Identity
pass: Head structures at the head end, and so on.
Regional identity is assigned along the axis.
fail: Every cell knew where it was and built the same thing anyway.
Position without identity: a coordinate nothing reads. Structures form, in the same form everywhere.

name: Make cells that are actually different
Differentiation
pass: Nerve, muscle and skin, all from the same genome.
Distinct cell types arise from one genome by selective expression.
fail: Correctly labelled regions, all made of identical cells.
Identity assigned but never executed: without selective expression the labels change nothing about the cells.

name: Have separate fingers
Sculpting
pass: The webbing between them is removed on purpose.
Interdigital tissue is cleared by programmed cell death.
fail: A working hand, with the fingers still joined together.
Everything correct and nothing removed. Your fingers are separated by cells being deliberately destroyed — building alone does not get you there.

win: An animal. Made by local rules, with no plan of it anywhere.
A complete body plan from five local mechanisms, none of which contains any representation of the finished organism.
lose: Read which test failed — it names exactly what was missing.
Each failed trial names the mechanism that was not in place. Reassign and re-test; the diagnosis is the lesson.

t: Building a body is done by local rules, and part of it is taking things away.
A body plan emerges from local rules — divide, sense position, take on identity, express selectively, and remove what is not needed.
Development is subtractive as well as additive. Sculpting by programmed cell death is not a tidying step; it is how several structures are made at all.

Apoptosis is a genuinely counter-intuitive component. Your fingers are separated because the cells between them are instructed to destroy themselves, and roughly half the neurons you ever make are eliminated during development. Building by removal is as fundamental here as building by addition.
sub: Nothing anywhere holds a picture of the finished animal.
There is no representation of the organism at any point in the process — only rules operating locally.
Which is why development is the clearest case in biology of global order from purely local interaction.

It is also why the genome is badly described as a blueprint. A blueprint maps one-to-one onto the thing built; a genome specifies processes whose outcome depends on their own execution. Recipe is closer, and even that flatters it.

q: Why do you have separate fingers?
How are digits separated during development?
What does interdigital apoptosis illustrate about development?
options: The cells between them were removed on purpose
The fingers grew outwards from a point
why: Your hand started as a paddle with no gaps. The cells in between were told to die, and that is what made the fingers separate.
The limb bud forms as a plate and the interdigital tissue is eliminated by programmed cell death. The fingers are not built apart; the space between them is taken away.

It shows that development is subtractive as well as additive, and that removal is instructed rather than incidental. Where the instruction fails, the digits remain joined — which is exactly what simple syndactyly is.

t: Understanding this is how anyone will ever grow a replacement organ.

Growing an organ means re-running development outside a body, and that requires knowing which local rules to supply and in what order. Organoids — small self-organising tissues grown from stem cells — work precisely because the cells still have the rules; given the right signals they build kidney and gut and brain tissue without being told what the finished thing should look like.
